planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained soil in full sun; Texas Lilac is a Texas Superstar-promoted chaste tree selection heavily marketed for extreme heat and drought toughness across Texas and the Gulf South.

directions: Root semi-hardwood cuttings in summer or plant container specimens in well-drained, average to poor soil in full sun; Texas Lilac is a widely promoted vitex selection valued for its dense, fragrant, lavender-blue flower spikes and reliably strong performance under the extreme heat, drought, and poor soil conditions typical of Texas and Gulf South summers, where it has become a landscape staple as a tough, low-maintenance flowering large shrub or small tree. It blooms heavily on new growth from late spring through fall, with the fragrant, gray-green palmately compound foliage adding a light sage-like scent to the garden. Cut back hard in late winter to about 12-18 inches above ground each year to encourage vigorous new growth and the best flower display, and to keep the plant at a manageable size. Bees and butterflies visit the long-lasting flower spikes heavily.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

common_name: Lime Sizzler Firebush (Variegated Chartreuse Hummingbird Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lime Sizzler is a Louisiana Super Plants selection, a variegated chartreuse-and-lime firebush cultivar that keeps the species' hummingbird-attracting orange-red flowers while adding colorful foliage.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Lime Sizzler is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated firebush selection with striking variegated foliage — leaves in bright chartreuse-lime with contrasting red-toned veining — that turns this reliable hummingbird shrub into a colorful foliage accent even between flushes of bloom. It keeps the tubular, red-orange flowers of the species, produced continuously from late spring through frost, which are a magnet for hummingbirds and butterflies throughout the long Gulf South growing season. In zone 9, it behaves as a root-hardy perennial in a well-protected, sheltered spot, dying back after a hard freeze and resprouting from the roots in spring, or it can be grown as a fast-filling warm-season annual shrub farther from the coast where winters are more severe. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, and prune out any winter-damaged wood in spring once new growth resumes.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Louisiana Super Plants Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Leslie Ann is a Louisiana Super Plants selection and 1961 Ralph Peer Camellia Award winner, a long-proven fall-blooming sasanqua for the Gulf South landscape.

directions: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun; Leslie Ann is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated sasanqua camellia with a long track record, having won the Ralph Peer Camellia Award back in 1961 and remaining a proven, reliable landscape performer in the decades since. It produces large, semi-double flowers combining pink, blush, and white in each bloom, opening from October through December when few other shrubs are in flower, and provides glossy evergreen structure through the rest of the year. Like other sasanquas it is more sun-tolerant and generally faster-growing than Camellia japonica, but still benefits from some afternoon shade and consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Louisiana Super Plants Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Florida Sunshine is a Louisiana Super Plants selection, a chartreuse-gold foliage sport of the Florida-native anise shrub, brightening further to yellow in fall and colder weather.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Florida Sunshine is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated selection of the Florida native anise shrub, grown almost entirely for its brilliant chartreuse-to-gold evergreen foliage, which glows in a shaded bed year-round and intensifies to a deeper yellow with cooler fall and winter temperatures — an unusually reliable, low-maintenance way to add sustained bright color to deep shade where flowering plants often struggle. Crushed leaves release the same anise-like fragrance as the straight species. Its narrow, upright growth habit makes it useful as a bright vertical accent or informal screen in a shaded border, contrasting well against dark-green companions like azaleas, camellias, or hollies. It tolerates a range of shade levels and adapts to both moist and average garden soil once established, needing little more than routine watering during dry spells and an occasional light shaping if a more formal look is wanted.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Louisiana Super Plants Program

common_name: Jane Magnolia (Little Girl Series Compact Late-Blooming Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Jane is a Louisiana Super Plants selection from the U.S. National Arboretum's 'Little Girl' hybrid magnolia series, bred to bloom later than star and saucer magnolias to help avoid late-frost flower damage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Jane is a Louisiana Super Plants-designated hybrid magnolia from the U.S. National Arboretum's 'Little Girl' breeding series (a cross of Magnolia liliiflora 'Nigra' and M. stellata 'Rosea'), producing large, fragrant, reddish-purple, tulip-shaped flowers with white interiors on a compact 10-15 foot tree — small enough to fit a modest yard where a full-size saucer magnolia would eventually overwhelm the space. Its key advantage over many early-spring-blooming magnolias is timing: it flowers noticeably later in spring than star and saucer magnolias, which often lose an entire season's bloom to a late freeze that damages open flowers, so Jane's later bloom window helps it dodge that common frustration. It sometimes produces a light rebloom later in summer as well. Give it a sheltered spot with consistent moisture and avoid heavy pruning, since magnolias generally need little routine shaping beyond removing dead or crossing wood.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Louisiana Super Plants Program
USDA Agricultural Research Service — National Arboretum Magnolia Breeding Program

common_name: Conversation Piece Azalea (Multi-Color Reblooming Robin Hill Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Conversation Piece was the first-ever Louisiana Super Plants selection (fall 2012), a Robin Hill series azalea noted for rebloom and flowers of several different colors and patterns appearing on the same plant at once.

directions: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Conversation Piece, the first-ever Louisiana Super Plants selection, is a Robin Hill series azalea known for a genuinely unusual trait — individual flowers on the same plant, and even within the same cluster, open in a range of colors and patterns, from soft pink to near-white to boldly splashed and variegated blooms, so no two flushes ever look quite the same and the shrub is a real conversation starter in bloom. It flowers in spring and often produces a second, lighter flush in fall, extending the display beyond the single spring bloom typical of most azaleas. Like other azaleas it needs consistently moist, well-drained, acidic soil and benefits from a partly shaded site protected from hot afternoon sun. Mulch to keep roots cool and moist, and prune lightly right after the spring bloom if shaping is needed, since next year's flower buds set on the current season's growth.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Louisiana Super Plants Program
